  - `Dim a(1) As New C1`: each element is made on its own first use. `a(1) Is Nothing` makes `a(1)`, and after
    `Set a(0) = Nothing` the next use makes another.
  - `ReDim b(1) As New C1` works the same way. It needs no Dim, even under Option Explicit (#1495).
  - For Each over the array, with a Variant loop variable, sees each untouched element as Nothing and makes none.
    After `Erase a`, the next use makes a new one.
  - An object loop variable over an array does not compile: "For Each control variable on arrays must be Variant".
- **A Type's field `m As New C1`** compiles. `t.m.Go` makes it, and `t.m Is Nothing` is False. `u = t` copies the
  reference, so `u.m Is t.m` is True and one object terminates.
- **`Static s As New C1`** in a Sub called twice makes one object, which terminates when the program ends.
- **In a class method, `Static s As New Collection`** is per instance: on one instance it counts 1 then 2, and on a second
  instance 1.

### What VB6 refuses to compile

| Declaration | VB6's compile error |
|---|---|
| `Dim x As New Integer`, `As New String`, `As New Variant`, `As New Object` | Syntax error |
| `Dim x As New E`, an Enum; `Dim x As New U`, a Type | Invalid use of New keyword |
| `Sub S(x As New C1)`; `Function F() As New C1` | Syntax error |
| `Dim d As New Collection`, then `d = 5` | Argument not optional |

### When the program ends

When Sub Main returns, the objects still held terminate: the Static's first, then the module variable's (#1490).

### What this overturned

- **That the declaration makes the object.** It was the issue's own assumption to check, and the reason to measure
  before pinning anything.
- **That For Each only writes its variable.** It reads it first, so an `As New` loop variable makes and drops an
  object, even when the loop runs no pass.

### What resisted explanation

- Why For Each reads a variable it is about to overwrite.
- Why a Type's field may be `As New` when a variable of a Type may not be.

### In HexIDE (#435)

**One mechanism, shared with a form's default instance (#822).**
- A Dim, Private or Public `As New` marks its slot with what it makes: a class's name, or "Collection".
- A read of the slot while it holds Nothing raises a request, `AutoInstanceNeeded`. The read path's retry loop, the one
  that already makes a form's default instance, answers it: `New` makes the object, it is stored, and the read is made
  again.
- An Initialize that raises leaves the slot Nothing, so the next use tries again.
- A read through a parameter, the one other name a slot is reached by, makes nothing.
- Locals and Watch read without asking, so looking makes no object. That is HexIDE's choice: what VB6's Locals window
  shows for an untouched `As New` variable was not measured.

**What reads count.**
- Every expression read counts. So do the Let target's read, `!` and `c(1) =` on a Collection, a module-qualified read,
  and For Each's first read of its variable.
- For's and For Each's own looks at the variable, to see it exists or release what it held, do not.

**Refused, by issue:**
- an array `As New` (#1482);
- a Type's field `As New` (#1488);
- `Static`, until #1491 made it run;
- `ReDim` of an undeclared name (#1495);
- `As New` of a type HexIDE has no class for, such as a form, by #435's own message.

**Known divergences the probes met, none of them `As New`'s:**
- #877: an `On Error` statement doesn't clear Err;
- #1006: `Set Module2.pm = Nothing` stores nothing;
- #1490: objects held at the end of the program don't terminate;
- #1493: `o = 5` released the object, until #1493.

**`AsNewTests`** pins five programs, seven compile errors and five refusals.

## Where VB6's designer puts a control's block (2026-10-23, #1481, design-time)

**The question.** `docs/vb6-designer-geometry.md` said that `Begin` order is z-order and that windowless controls have a
plane of their own. The direction was measured only for two Lines (`docs/vb6-fidelity-oracle.md`, "The Line control"),
and nothing recorded where VB6's designer writes a control it adds or reorders. HexIDE drew the last block on top and
wrote a new control's block last.

**The probe.** A form, opened in VB6's IDE through the console agent. Its blocks were Picture1 (red), Picture2 (blue),
then Frame1 holding Picture3 (green) and Picture4 (yellow). The two pictures in each pair overlapped. After each step
below I saved with File > Save, read the form-level and Frame-level block order from VB6's file, and took a
screenshot.

| Step | What VB6 showed | Blocks VB6 then wrote |
|---|---|---|
| Opened, then F5 | red over blue, green over yellow, at design time and at run time | Picture1, Picture2, Frame1 (Picture3, Picture4) |
| Bring to Front on Picture2 | blue over red | **Picture2**, Picture1, Frame1 (Picture3, Picture4) |
| Send to Back on Picture3 | yellow over green | Picture2, Picture1, Frame1 (Picture4, **Picture3**) |
| Click inside Frame1, then double-click the CommandButton tool | Command1 at the form's centre, over Frame1 | **Command1**, Picture2, Picture1, Frame1 (...) |
| Draw a CommandButton inside Frame1 | Command2 in the Frame | ..., Frame1 (**Command2**, Picture4, Picture3) |
| Copy Frame1, paste, No to each array prompt | the copy at 0, 0, its contents the other way up: green over yellow | **Frame2 (Picture6, Picture5, Command3)**, Command1, ... |
| Double-click the Label tool | Label1 at the form's centre, hidden under Command1 at the same place | ..., Frame1 (...), **Label1** |
| Draw a second Label | Label2 | ..., Frame1 (...), **Label2**, Label1 |
| Send to Back on Label2 | | ..., Frame1 (...), Label1, **Label2** |
| Bring to Front on Label2 | | ..., Frame1 (...), **Label2**, Label1 |
| Send to Back on Command1 | | Frame2 (...), Picture2, Picture1, Frame1 (...), **Command1**, Label2, Label1 |

In the pasted Frame2, Picture6 is the copy of Picture3, Picture5 of Picture4, and Command3 of Command2. Their TabIndexes
were 8 for Command3, 9 for Picture5 and 10 for Picture6. The array prompts came in the source's order: Frame1, Command2,
Picture4, Picture3.

**What it shows:**
- **The first block in a container is its top control,** in VB6's designer and in the running form alike.
- **Each container's blocks run windowed controls first, then windowless ones** (Label, Shape, Line, Image). A
  windowless control is drawn under every windowed control in its container, whatever the order: Label1, written
  last, was hidden under Command1. The VB98 template corpus agrees, 60 windowed blocks before any windowless sibling
  and none after one.
- **A new or pasted control goes first in its plane's run.** A windowed control goes first in its container, and a
  Label goes first among the Labels, after every windowed control.
- **Bring to Front and Send to Back move a block to the start or the end of its plane's run.** A Label stays behind
  the windowed controls, a windowed control sent to back stays ahead of the Labels, and a container takes what it
  holds. Neither changes the TabIndex.
- **A pasted container's contents come out the other way up.** VB6 pastes them one at a time, in the source's order,
  and each goes on top. So the copy stacks them in reverse, while its names and TabIndexes follow the source's order.
- **Double-clicking a tool after a click inside a Frame adds the control to the form**, not to the Frame. Whether the
  click had selected the Frame was not captured.

**In HexIDE (#1481):**
- **What follows the measurements:**
  - The designer draws each container's first block on top.
  - A new or pasted control is written first in its plane.
  - Bring to Front and Send to Back move a control within its plane, with what it holds.
  - A loaded form is saved in the order it was read.
- **One deliberate divergence:** a pasted container keeps its source's stacking. A copy that turns its contents over
  is an artefact of pasting them one at a time, not a design, so HexIDE does not reproduce it.
- **Two gaps, filed:**
  - The running form still draws the last block on top (#1497, since fixed: "How a running form stacks its
    controls").
  - A control added in front of one HexIDE carries as text is written after it (#1498, since fixed: "A control VB6
    knows and HexIDE carries stacks with the rest").

**Not measured:**
- A Shape, Line or Image beside a Label in the windowless plane. Only Labels were tried.
- Bring to Front with several controls selected.
- A paste while a container is selected.
- The `ZOrder` method at run time.

## A control VB6 knows and HexIDE carries stacks with the rest (2026-10-23, #1498, design-time, IDE, release build)

**The question.** The rule above was measured on intrinsic controls only. HexIDE carries a control it does not model as
the text it was read as, written back where it was read, so the designer never sees it. Does VB6 stack an OCX control
like the others?

**The probe.** VB6's own `Template\Forms\Web Browser.frm` in a one-form Standard EXE project, with `MSCOMCTL.OCX` and
`ieframe.dll` referenced. Its form-level blocks are `tbToolBar` (`MSComctlLib.Toolbar`), `brwWebBrowser`
(`SHDocVwCtl.WebBrowser`), `timTimer`, `picAddress` (holding `cboAddress` and `lblAddress`), then `imlIcons`
(`MSComctlLib.ImageList`). HexIDE models only the Timer, the PictureBox and what it holds. Through the console agent:
the project opened (VB6 raised "Error accessing the system registry" once, dismissed with Enter), Ctrl+R, the form,
Shift+F7, a real double-click on the CommandButton tool, a click on the new button, then the step below through the
Format menu's Order submenu, a click on the designer, and Ctrl+S. Each run started from a fresh copy of the template.

| Step | Form-level blocks VB6 wrote |
|---|---|
| CommandButton added | **Command1**, tbToolBar, brwWebBrowser, timTimer, picAddress, imlIcons |
| Added, then Send to Back | tbToolBar, brwWebBrowser, timTimer, picAddress, imlIcons, **Command1** |
| Added, Send to Back, then Bring to Front | **Command1**, tbToolBar, brwWebBrowser, timTimer, picAddress, imlIcons |

After Send to Back the button was hidden under the WebBrowser, its selection handles still showing.

**What it shows:**
- **An OCX control stacks with the intrinsic ones.** A new control goes in front of the toolbar, and Send to Back puts
  it behind the ImageList, a control with no window at run time. The Timer and the ImageList count as windowed: Send
  to Back went past both.
- **Nothing else moves.** Each step changed only Command1's place. `picAddress`'s own blocks were untouched.

**What HexIDE did:** a carried block kept the place it was read at, so the added button went in after the toolbar and
the WebBrowser, and the ImageList, read fifth, was written ahead of `picAddress`, a control nobody had moved. Send to
Back and Bring to Front moved a control past the modelled controls only.

**In HexIDE (#1498):** each control in the designer counts the carried controls in its container that are stacked under
it, read from the file on load. A control added, pasted or brought to front goes over all of them, and one sent to back
under them. A save turns the counts back into where each carried block goes, through the same placement the writer
uses, so a form loaded and saved untouched comes back byte for byte.

**Inferred, not measured:** a carried block VB6 wrote after a Label is taken to be windowless, since VB6 writes every
windowed block first. A windowed control sent to back stays over such a block, and a Label sent to back goes under it.
No corpus file has a carried block after a windowless one.

## Static (2026-10-23, #1491)

**The question.** `Static n As Long` stopped the program: "non dim variables not supported". The `Static` keyword on a
procedure was parsed and then ignored, so a `Static Sub`'s locals started again at zero on every call: silently wrong.
#1491 asked what a Static keeps and for how long:
- its first value;
- recursion;
- a `Static Sub` or `Function`;
- arrays;
- a class's and a form's Statics, and when they end.

**The probe.**
- Two Sub Main programs, the second with four classes and a form, made native and p-code under en-GB.
- 34 one-statement compile projects.
- Two two-form projects started from Form1, the second without `New Form2`.
- `StaticTests`' 4 transcript programs and 2 parse refusals, and the form project `StaticInFormTests` runs, made the same
  way. They logged exactly what the tests pin, and gave the compile errors the tests expect.

Native code and p-code agreed on every line.

### What a Static keeps

| Program | VB6 |
|---|---|
| a Sub with `Static n As Long: n = n + 1`, called three times | 1, 2, 3 |
| two Subs, each with its own `Static n` | separate: 10, 20 in the second while the first counts on |
| a recursive Sub, `Static n`, three levels deep, then called again | 1, 2, 3 on the way down; 3 at every level on the way back; 4 on the next call. **One slot for every frame** |
| `Private Static Sub` with `Dim a As Long` and `Dim s As String` | 1, then 2; "z", then "zz" |
| `Private Static Function F() As Long` with `Dim m`, and `F = F + 1` | `m` counts 1, 2; **`F` is 1 on every call**: a Static Function's own return value is not Static |
| `Bump n`, passing the Static ByRef to a Sub that adds 100 | 100, then 200 |
| `Static q` inside a `For` run three times, `q = q + 1` | 3, then 6: the statement re-run does nothing |
| `Static u` inside an `If` that is never taken | `u` exists and counts 1, 2 |

### First values, and what it holds

- Each type starts at its own zero:
  - Integer, Long, Byte: 0, with TypeName Integer, Long, Byte;
  - Boolean: False;
  - Single, Double, Currency: TypeName Single, Double, Currency;
  - Date: 0;
  - String: "";
  - Variant and untyped: Empty;
  - `As Object`, a class and `As Collection`: Nothing;
  - `fa(2) As Long`: `Long()`, UBound 2;
  - `da() As Long`: `Long()`;
  - a Type: its fields' zeros.
- Every kind keeps what it was given:
  - a fixed array's element;
  - a dynamic array grown by `ReDim Preserve`;
  - a Type's fields;
  - a String;
  - a Variant;
  - an object, and a Collection with its items.
- `Erase` of a Static fixed array zeros it, and of a dynamic one deallocates it. The next call finds `fa(0)` 0 again,
  and the array as it was ReDimmed last.

### A class's, and a form's

| Program | VB6 |
|---|---|
| two instances of a class, each calling a method with `Static n` | each counts from 1: **a class's Statics are its instance's** |
| `Static times` in Class_Initialize | 1 for each instance |
| a `Public Static Sub` in a class | per instance |
| a Static in a Private method reached through a Public one | per instance, as if called directly |
| `Set k = Nothing` on an instance holding a field object and three methods' Static objects, made in the order Hold, B, A | Class_Terminate, then the field's object, then the Statics' in the module's order, **Hold, A, B**, not the order they were made |
| a form's `Public Sub Tick()` with `Static n`, after `Load Form2` | 1, 2 |
| `Unload Form2`, then `Form2.Tick` | 3: **a Static survives Unload** |
| `Set Form2 = Nothing` (Form_Terminate), then `Form2.Tick` | 1: a new instance starts again |
| `New Form2`, loaded, `Tick` twice | 1, 2: its own |
| a Sub's `Static t As C` still holding its object when Sub Main returns | the object terminates as the program ends (#1490) |

### Static As New

`As New` works on a Static as it does on a Dim (#435), and the object it makes is kept from call to call:

| Program | VB6 |
|---|---|
| `Static s As New Made`, then `s.Name = s.Name & "x"`, three calls | made once, at the first call's use; "x", "xx", "xxx" |
| the third call ending `Set s = Nothing` | it terminates there |
| `Static c As New Made`, with `Set c = Nothing` at the end of the first call | the second call makes a new one, its Name "" |
| a class method with `Static c As New Collection: c.Add 1`, twice on one instance and once on a second | 1, 2, then 1 |

### What VB6 refuses to compile

| Declaration | VB6's compile error |
|---|---|
| `Static n As Long` at a standard module's level, or a class module's | Invalid outside procedure |
| `Dim n` then `Static n` in one procedure; `Static n` twice | Duplicate declaration in current scope |
| `Private Sub S(Static x As Long)` | Syntax error |
| `Sub S(Static x As Long)`, at the top of the module | Expected: identifier |
| `Static Const C = 1` | Syntax error |
| `Dim L As Long` in a Sub, then a call of the module's Sub `L` | Expected Sub, Function, or Property: the local hides the procedure, so the call no longer names one |

Every `Static` form compiles: a fixed or dynamic array, a Type, a Date, an untyped Static, `As Object`, `As Collection`,
a class, and two names on one line.

### What this overturned

- **That a Static Function's own name is Static too.** Its other locals are, and its return value starts at its zero on
  every call.
- **That a class's Statics are released as they were made.** They are released in the order the module declares them,
  after the fields.

### What resisted explanation

- Why `Sub S(Static x As Long)` is "Expected: identifier" at the top of a module, and "Syntax error" when the Sub is
  Private further down.

### In HexIDE (#1491)

**What it does:**
- A Static local's slot is made the first time its procedure declares it, and found again by the declaration's own parse
  node at every later call, a recursive one included. The call never releases it.
- A standard module's procedures keep their Statics for the run.
- A class's or a form's are kept per instance. When the instance terminates, they are released after its fields, in
  source order.
- A `Static Sub`, `Function` or `Property` makes every Dim local Static. Its parameters and a Function's return value are
  not.
- `Static` outside a procedure is "Invalid outside procedure". A Static parameter or a `Static Const` does not parse.

**Known divergences:**
- #1490: a standard module's Static, like a module variable, keeps its object past the end of the program.
- A duplicate `Dim` or `Static` in one procedure is not refused (#1499). The first declaration wins.
- `New Form2` is #822, so the form test leaves out the second instance.

**What pins it:**
- `StaticTests` pins four programs and three refusals.
- `StaticInFormTests` pins the form program.

## A Let into an object variable (2026-10-23, #1493)

**The obvious guess is that `k = 5`, with `k As C1` holding an instance, replaces the object with 5. It assigns the
default member of the object `k` holds.** A class with none raises 438, and `k` keeps the object. Holding Nothing,
the same Let raises 91. A Variant is different: it takes the value and drops the object.

**The question.** HexIDE released the object at `k = 5`, so its Terminate ran there, and stored 5. The program ran on
with the object gone, and `k.Name` on the next line failed to compile. #1493 asked which targets are object variables
for a Let, and what each does.

**The probe.**
- Two Sub Main programs, made native and p-code under en-GB.
- The 3 programs `LetIntoObjectTests` runs, made the same way. They logged exactly what the tests pin.

Native code and p-code agreed on every line. `C1` logs its Initialize and Terminate.

### Object variables

| Target, holding an instance of `C1`, which has no default member | VB6 |
|---|---|
| `Dim k As C1`: `k = 5`, and `k = "x"` | 438 both times; `k` still the instance |
| `Dim o As Object`: `o = 5` | 438; `o` still the instance |
| `Dim an As New C1`, untouched: `an = 5` | the instance is made, then 438 (#435) |
| a ByRef parameter `x As C1`: `x = 6` | 438; the caller's variable still the instance |
| a ByRef or ByVal parameter `x As Object`, and a ByVal `x As C1` | 438 |
| `Function F() As C1`, holding an instance: `F = 7` | 438; the Function returns the instance |
| `Function FObject() As Object`, the same | 438; it returns the instance |
| a class's `Public o As C1`: `h.o = 8`, and `.o = 9` in `With h` | 438; the field still the instance |
| a class's `Private mo As C1`, from inside: `mo = 5` | 438 |

| Target, holding Nothing | VB6 |
|---|---|
| `Dim n As C1`: `n = 5` | 91; `n` still Nothing |
| `Dim o2 As Object`: `o2 = 5` | 91 |

### Variants

| Target, holding an instance | VB6 |
|---|---|
| `Dim v As Variant`: `v = 5` | no error. The instance terminates at the Let, and `v` is 5, an Integer |
| an untyped `u`, and a class's `Public v As Variant` | the same |
| a ByRef `x As Variant`, and a ByVal untyped `x` | the same |
| `Function FVariant() As Variant` and an untyped Function, holding an instance | the same, and the Function returns the Integer |

### A default member

`d = 11`, with `d` holding an instance of a class whose `Property Get Value` carries `Attribute Value.VB_UserMemId = 0`,
calls its `Property Let Value` with 11. There is no error, and `d.Value` is 11 afterwards.

### Aside: a variable that hides a procedure

The first probe declared a local `r As C1` in Sub Main while the module had a Sub `R` that logs. Every `R "label"` then
named the variable. It compiled, and under `On Error Resume Next` it raised and logged nothing. A `Dim L As Long` in
the same position is a compile error ("Expected Sub, Function, or Property", #1491's probes). So an object variable
standing where a procedure call should be compiles, as a late call of its default member, and a Long does not.

### What this overturned

- **That a Let into an object variable replaces what it holds.** Only a Variant's does. Any declared object variable
  hands the value to its object's default member, and keeps the object whatever happens.
- **That `As Object` is a Variant for this purpose.** It reads late, as a Variant does (#1005), but a Let into it is
  438, as into a class-typed variable.

### In HexIDE (#1493)

**What counts as an object variable.** A Let target is one when it is any of:
- declared as a class, `As Object` or `As Collection`;
- an `As Object` parameter (`ExecutionEnvironment.ObjectParameters`, new);
- any other slot that holds an object and isn't a Variant's.

**What a Let into one does.** It refuses before anything is released or stored:
- 438 for a class with no default member, and for a Collection;
- 91 for Nothing;
- a refusal naming #174 for a class with a default member;
- a refusal naming #790 for a control.

**Where it was hard to tell a Variant apart.** An untyped or `As Variant` Function's own name takes the value. Its
slot has no Variant mark, so the executor is told (`VariantReturn`). `ProcedureInfo.ReturnsObject` and
`ParamInfo.DeclaredObject` now separate `As Object` from Variant, where `ReturnsVariant` and `ReadsAsVariant` had
counted it as one for reading.

**Not covered:**
- a Type's field declared as a class;
- an element of an object array (#1482).

**`LetIntoObjectTests`** pins three programs and the default-member refusal.

**#169 found one more.** An object Function's return name started Empty before any Set. So `F = 5` in `F() As Object`
took the value where vb6.exe raises 91, and an unset `As Object` or `As Collection` Function returned Empty. It starts
Nothing now, and `LetIntoObjectTests` pins a fourth program.

## The size of a control added from the toolbox (2026-10-23, #1473, design-time, IDE, release build)

**The question.** "Where the Format commands put a control" measured where VB6 puts a CommandButton added by
double-clicking its tool: 1215 x 495, centred, then on the grid. HexIDE gave every class 50 x 50 pixels (750 x 750
twips). Each class needed its own measurement.

**The probe.** An empty 6000 x 4500 form with the default 120-twip grid, in VB6's IDE. I double-clicked every intrinsic
tool except OLE, whose double-click opens a dialog, clicking an empty corner of the form first each time, then saved.
Every control went onto the form, none into another. The values are VB6's file.

| Class | Width x Height | Left, Top |
|---|---|---|
| CommandButton, Label, TextBox, Frame, CheckBox, OptionButton, PictureBox, Shape, Image | 1215 x 495 | 2400, 2040 |
| ComboBox | 1215 x 315 | 2400, 2040 |
| ListBox | 1215 x 450 | 2400, 2040 |
| HScrollBar | 1215 x 255 | 2400, 2160 |
| VScrollBar | 255 x 1335 | 2880, 1560 |
| DriveListBox | 1215 x 315 | 2400, 2040 |
| DirListBox | 1215 x 315 | 2400, 2040 |
| FileListBox | 1215 x 480 | 2400, 2040 |
| Data | 1215 x 300 | 2400, 2160 |
| Timer | none written | 2400, 2040 |
| Line | X1 2400, Y1 2040, X2 3600, Y2 2520 | |

**What it shows:**
- **Most classes take 1215 x 495.** The ComboBox, the list boxes, the scroll bars and the Data control each have a size
  of their own.
- **Each is centred by its own size, halves truncated, then put on the grid, a half going up.** For example, the
  VScrollBar: 3000 - 127 = 2873, on the grid 2880; and 2250 - 667 = 1583, on the grid 1560. The Data control is
  2250 - 150 = 2100, 17.5 units, which goes up to 2160.
- **A Timer writes no size, but is placed as a 1215 x 495 control would be.**
- **A Line is a diagonal** from the centred, gridded corner, 1200 across and 480 down.
- **A click with a tool selected and no drag adds nothing.** The CommandButton tool was pressed, a click on the form
  made no control, and the toolbox went back to the pointer.

**In HexIDE (#1473):**
- A control added by a double-click takes its class's size and is placed by it, for every class the toolbox holds.
- A click without a drag already added nothing.
- The DriveListBox, DirListBox, FileListBox, Data, Image and Line rows wait for those controls to reach the toolbox;
  the Image's is already the default.

**Not measured:**
- A form with another font, which may change the ComboBox's and the list boxes' heights.
- A grid other than 120 twips.
- A double-click while a container is selected, measured only as "after a click inside a Frame" ("Where VB6's designer
  puts a control's block").

## An undeclared variable passed ByRef (2026-10-23, #1505)

Measured on vb6.exe, native and p-code identical, under en-GB, with no `Option Explicit`. Each program
`ByRefUndeclaredTests` pins was made as written.

A name nothing claims, passed as an argument, is declared where it is passed, as a Let would declare it. A ByRef
parameter then writes into it.

| probe | result |
|---|---|
| `Bump a12` twice, with `Sub Bump(x)` doing `x = x + 1` | `a12` is an Integer 2 |
| `Fill b12`, with `Sub Fill(ByRef s)` doing `s = "filled"` | String "filled" |
| `Fill s:=c12`, the same by name | String "filled" |
| `r = BumpF(d12)`, a Function that adds 1 to `x` and returns `x * 10` | `d12` an Integer 1, `r` 10 |
| `Bump (f12)` | Empty: the parentheses pass a copy |
| `Keep h12`, with `Sub Keep(ByVal x)` doing `x = 9` | Empty |
| `Bump Seven`, with `Function Seven()` returning 7 | `Seven` is still 7: a Function's name is called, not declared |
| `BumpI i12` twice under `DefInt I`, with `Sub BumpI(x As Integer)` | an Integer 2 |
| `k.Bump e12` twice, a class's `Sub Bump(x)` | an Integer 2 |

**The obvious guess, and HexIDE had made it.** A read of an undeclared name is Empty, so an argument would be only a
value. It is not: VB6 declares the variable at the argument, so the procedure's write lands in it.

### In HexIDE (#1505)

`ExpressionExecutor.ResolveArg` passes a ByRef parameter the caller's slot when the argument is a variable
(`TryGetArgLocation`). A name never declared had no slot, because the read path deliberately declares nothing, so that
a watch expression cannot create a variable (#171). The argument was therefore passed as a copy.

The read now records the bare name it found unclaimed (`unclaimedRead`). When that is the argument being resolved,
`DeclareUnclaimed` declares it with `StatementExecutor.AllocImplicitVariable`, the same helper a store uses, so a DefType
still applies. A watch or Immediate-window evaluation still declares nothing: it suppresses implicit declaration, so the
read refuses before it records anything, and it refuses user procedure calls anyway.

## Chr, Asc, ChrW and AscW (2026-10-23, #1134)

Measured on vb6.exe, native and p-code identical, on a machine whose ANSI code page is 1252, under en-GB. Each program
`CharacterCodeTests` pins was made as written.

**Chr and Asc go through the ANSI code page; ChrW and AscW do not.** HexIDE had Chr and Asc working in UTF-16 units,
which agrees with VB6 only below &H80 and, by coincidence, from &HA0 to &HFF.

| probe | result |
|---|---|
| `AscW(Chr(&H80))` | 8364: "€" |
| `AscW(Chr(&H81))`, `&H8D`, `&H8F`, `&H90`, `&H9D` | 129, 141, 143, 144, 157: a byte 1252 leaves undefined is its own code point |
| `AscW(Chr(&H9F))` | 376: "Ÿ" |
| `AscW(Chr(&HA0))`, `AscW(Chr(255))` | 160, 255 |
| `Chr(256)`, `Chr(-1)`, `Chr(32767)`, `Chr(True)` | 5 each |
| `Chr(3000000000#)` | 6 |
| `Chr(Null)` | 94 |
| `Chr("x")` | 13; `Chr("66")` is "B" |
| `AscW(Chr(65.5))`, `AscW(Chr(66.5))` | 66, 66: half to even |
| `Len(Chr(0))`, `Len(Chr(Empty))` | 1, 1 |
| `Asc(ChrW(8364))` | 128 |
| `Asc(ChrW(&H81))`, `Asc(ChrW(&H178))`, `Asc(ChrW(&H2019))` | 129, 159, 146 |
| `Asc(ChrW(&H100))` | **65**: Ā best-fits to "A" |
| `Asc(ChrW(&H416))` | 63: Ж has no fit, so "?" |
| `Asc("AB")`, `Asc(65)`, `Asc(True)` | 65, 54, 84: the argument is made text first |
| `Asc("")`, `Asc(Empty)` | 5, 5 |
| `Asc(Null)` | 94 |
| `AscW(ChrW(&H20AC))` | 8364 |
| `AscW(ChrW(&HF050))`, `AscW(ChrW(61520))` | -4016, -4016: `&HF050` is an Integer, -4016, taken as its unsigned unit |
| `ChrW(-4016) = ChrW(61520)` | True |
| `AscW(ChrW(65535))`, `AscW(ChrW(-32768))`, `AscW(ChrW(True))` | -1, -32768, -1 |
| `ChrW(65536)`, `ChrW(-32769)` | 5, 5 |
| `ChrW(3000000000#)` | 6 |
| `ChrW(Null)`, `AscW(Null)` | 94, 94 |
| `AscW(ChrW(65.5))` | 66 |
| `Len(ChrW(Empty))`, `Len(ChrW(&HD800))`, `Len(ChrW(0))` | 1, 1, 1: a lone surrogate is one unit |
| `AscW("AB")`, `AscW(66)`, `AscW(1.5)` | 65, 54, 49 |
| `AscW("")`, `AscW(Empty)` | 5, 5 |
| `ChrW(CharCode:=65)`, `AscW(String:="A")` | "A", 65 |
| `ChrW(Code:=65)`, `AscW(Str:="A")` | do not compile: "Named argument not found" |
| `ChrW()`, `AscW()` | do not compile: "Argument not optional" (HexIDE: #1512) |
| `AscW$("A")` | does not compile: "Type-declaration character does not match declared data type" |
| `TypeName(AscW("A"))`, `TypeName(Asc("A"))`, `TypeName(ChrW(65))` | Integer, Integer, String |

**Typed or Variant**, by #987's probe:
- `AscW("A")` against `Case Is < 65.4` takes Case Else, and `AscW("A") * 7000` is 6: typed, as `Asc` is.
- `AscW(v)`, with `v` a Variant holding "A", behaves the same way.
- `ChrW(57)` against `Case Is > 10` takes Case Else: a Variant, as `Chr` is.

**Every `$` form that answers text answers a typed String.** "9" from each of them, against `Case Is > 10`, takes the
Case: `Chr$(57)`, `ChrW$(57)`, `Format$(9)`, `Hex$(9)`, `LCase$("9")`, `Left$("9", 1)`, `LTrim$("9")`, `Mid$("9", 1)`,
`Oct$(9)`, `Right$("9", 1)`, `RTrim$("9")`, `String$(1, "9")`, `Trim$("9")` and `UCase$("9")`. `Str$(19)`, which is
" 19", takes Case Else, which is the typed reading the other way round. Their plain forms are Variants: `Mid("9", 1)`,
`Left("9", 1)`, `Format(9)` and `Hex(9)` take Case Else, and **`Str(19)` takes the Case**, read as 19.

**Print # best-fits too.** `Print #` of Ā, Ж and ’ to a file opened For Output writes the bytes 65, 63 and 146, read back
with `Get`. So the earlier row "`ChrW$(&H416)` is written as '?'" is true, but Ж has no fit, so it could not tell a
best fit from a plain replacement. HexIDE wrote Ā as "?" until #1511.

**Not measured here:**
- **A double-byte ANSI code page** (932). VB6 is documented to give `Chr` a range of -32768 to 65535 there, a code above
  255 being a lead and a trail byte, and `Asc` a possibly negative pair. Unmeasured, so HexIDE refuses a code beyond
  ASCII under one (#1509).
- **ChrB and the rest of the byte-string family.** A first `ChrB` probe did not compile. HexIDE's strings cannot hold a
  one-byte string at all (#1510).

### In HexIDE (#1134)

`VB6BuiltIns.ChrInCodePage` decodes a byte with the ANSI code page's table, and `AscInCodePage` encodes with that
table's own fallbacks, best fit among them. Both take the code page from `Vb6TextEncoding.Ansi`, so a Debug build's
`--ansi-code-page` reaches them, and both refuse beyond ASCII when the table is double-byte. `CharCode` and
`FirstCharacterOf` hold the argument rules the four share.

`ExpressionExecutor`'s typed list gains `AscW`, its Variant list `ChrW` and `Str`, and its list of `$` forms that do not
compile gains `AscW`. `DollarResult` now marks its String typed.

## The name VB6's designer gives a new control (2026-10-23, #540, design-time, IDE, release build)

**The question.** HexIDE named the first CommandButton on a form Command0, and a pasted control took its number from
the count of controls on the canvas. The common recollection is that VB6 starts at 1, and #929's probe saw Command1.
Still open: whether VB6 fills a gap or counts on from the highest number, whether a number freed by a delete comes
back, and whether a paste follows the same rule.

**The probe.** A form saved holding Command1, Command3 and Text5, opened in VB6's IDE. Each step below was saved, and
the names are VB6's file. To add a control, I clicked an empty part of the form, then double-clicked the tool. To
paste, I selected the control, used Edit > Copy and Edit > Paste, and answered **No** to "You already have a control
named 'Command3'. Do you want to create a control array?".

| Form before | Step | New name |
|---|---|---|
| Command1, Command3, Text5 | add a CommandButton | **Command2** |
| Command1, Command2, Command3, Text5 | add a TextBox | **Text1** |
| Command1, Command3, Text5 | paste Command3 | **Command2**, caption still "Command3" |
| Command1, Command2, Command3, Text5 | paste Text5 | **Text1**, Text still "Text5" |
| Command1, Command2, Command3, Text1, Text5, after Command4 was pasted and deleted | add a CommandButton | **Command4** |
| Command1, Command3, Text5, after Command2 was added and deleted | add a CommandButton | **Command2** |

**What it shows:**
- **A new or pasted control takes its class's prefix and the lowest number from 1 that no control on the form has.**
  It fills a gap a file left (Command2 beside Command1 and Command3), and it does not count on from the highest
  number (Text1 beside Text5).
- **A number freed by a delete comes back**, in the middle (Command2) and at the top (Command4). So VB6 doesn't keep a
  per-session counter, which would have given Command5. The name depends only on what is on the form.
- **A paste answered No follows the same rule, and keeps the copied caption or text.** Only the name is new.

**In HexIDE (#540):**
- Both routes now name a control the same way, from 1. A new control used to start at 0, and a paste at the number of
  controls on the canvas.
- A name a preserved control holds still counts as taken (#854).
- HexIDE's paste never asks the array question. It does what VB6's No does.

**Not measured:**
- A paste answered **Yes**, which makes a control array.
- Several controls pasted at once, where each presumably takes the lowest free number in turn.
- A gap in a control array's indexes.

## Debug.Assert (2026-10-23, #1467)

Measured with vb6.exe in two places. The IDE was driven with `vb6.exe /runexit`, in session 0 as the `/make` probes are,
and the compiled EXE was built both native and p-code, the two agreeing. Each program the tests pin was run as written.

**In the IDE, release build**, `Debug.Assert X` with `L` logging each side of it. These rows ran on the oracle's IDE,
VB6.EXE 6.00.8176 with VBA6.DLL 6.0.8169, which is VB6's original release and not SP6 (#1524). Re-measure them once SP6
is installed. The compiled-EXE rows below ran on MSVBVM60 6.00.9848, SP6's runtime, and stand.

| X | result |
|---|---|
| `True`, `5`, `-1`, `"True"` | goes on |
| `F()`, returning True and logging "F called" | goes on; F is called |
| `False`, `0`, `Empty`, `Null`, `"False"` | break mode at the statement |
| `G()`, returning False and logging "G called" | G is called, then break mode |
| `"abc"` | 13, which On Error Resume Next traps |
| `1 / 0` | 11, trapped |
| `False`, or `G()`, under On Error Resume Next | still break mode |

So the condition is read as `If` reads it (#847): Null and Empty do not hold, where `CBool(Null)` raises 94.

**Telling break mode from an error.** A project that breaks leaves the IDE waiting, which `/runexit` cannot end, so the
probe's timeout reports it, with nothing logged after the assertion. An error dialog would wait the same way. So each
waiting case was also run under On Error Resume Next: there an error is trapped and the next line logs it, as "abc" and
`1 / 0` show. Null, Empty, 0 and "False" still waited, so they break rather than raise.

**Not measured:** what Continue (F5) does after the break, since session 0 has no one to press it. HexIDE goes on with
the statement after the assertion, as it does after `Stop`.

**In a compiled EXE**, native and p-code:

| statement | result |
|---|---|
| `Debug.Assert False` | skipped |
| `Debug.Assert G()` | skipped, and **G is never called** |
| `Debug.Assert "abc"`, `Debug.Assert 1 / 0` | skipped: nothing is raised |
| `Debug.Print F()` | **F is called**, though nothing is printed |

The two `Debug` statements differ here. The compiler removes `Debug.Assert` with its argument, but evaluates
`Debug.Print`'s arguments and discards only the printing. "Debug statements are removed at compile time", as the issue
had it, is true of the first and not of the second.

**Compile errors:** `Debug.Assert` with no condition, and `Debug.Assert True, False`, are each "Syntax error". A compile
error is the compiler's answer, so these came from the release build's compiler even in a `/make` (#1524).

### In HexIDE (#1467)

`StatementExecutor` takes `Debug.Assert` as a statement beside `Debug.Print`:
- **With a debugger** (`DebugController`, which every IDE run has), it evaluates the condition with `ConditionHolds`, the
  same reading `If` uses. When the condition does not hold it suspends through
  `IDebugController.EnterBreakFromAssertionAsync`.
- **Headless** (the Make EXE runner and the test fixture), it returns before evaluating anything, as `Stop` ends the
  program there.

The break carries a new `StopReason.Assertion`, which `get_debug_state` and `run_project`'s note report.
`Call Debug.Assert(x)` reaches `DebugProxy.Call` with no statement to break at, and is refused, naming the statement
form.

**A reusable harness.** `vb6.exe /runexit project.vbp`, run in the guest with a timeout, measures what the VB6 IDE does
rather than the compiler: in the oracle as it stands, the release build's IDE (#1524). A project that ends
logs to its end. One that waits is in break mode or showing a dialog, and
running it again under On Error Resume Next tells the two apart.

## Indexing a call's result (2026-10-23, #1476)

Measured with `/make` in four batches, native and p-code identical on every row. A row that printed something is a
run-time result of a built EXE on SP6's MSVBVM60. A compile error came from the oracle's release-build compiler (#1524).
Each line printed `TypeName` and the value, or the error.

### Reading

| expression | vb6.exe |
|---|---|
| `Split("x y z")(0)`, `(2)`, `(3)` | x, z, 9 |
| `Split(s, " ")(1)` | y |
| `Array(1, 2)(1)` | Integer 2 |
| `V3()(2)` and `V3()(-1)`, with `V3() As Variant` returning `Array(10, 20, 30)` | 30, and 9 |
| `T3()(1)`, with `T3() As Long()` | Long 200: the typed array's element |
| `Jag()(1)(0)` and `Jag()(1)(1)(1)`, with `Jag` returning `Array(Array(1, 2), Array(3, Array(4, 5)))` | 3 and 5 |
| `WithArg(4)(2)`, with `WithArg(n)` returning `Array(n, n * 2, n * 3)` | 12 |
| `NoArgs()(1)`, with `NoArgs() As Variant` returning `Array(5, 6)` | 6 |
| `Col()(2)` and `Col()("a")`, with `Col() As Collection` | beta, alpha: the Collection's Item |
| `VScalar()(0)` and `VStr()(0)`, Variant Functions returning 42 and "abc" | 13 |
| `Split(s)(0, 1)` | 9: the wrong number of subscripts |
| `Split(s)("1")`, `Split(s)(1.5)` | y, z: an index converts as any subscript does, 1.5 rounding to 2 |
| `k.Items()(1)`, `k.Typed()(2)`, `k.Bag()(2)`, `k.Echo("m n")(1)`, `k.Prop()(0)` | the method's or Property Get's result, indexed |

### A parameterless procedure given arguments

Each was its own project: a `Private Function F` in the same module, called from `Sub Main` as `r = F(...)` under
On Error Resume Next.

| F | call | vb6.exe |
|---|---|---|
| `Function F()` or `Function F() As Variant`, returning `Array(5, 6)` | `F(1)` | Integer 6 |
| the same | `F(5, 6)` | 9 |
| `Function F()` or `As Variant`, returning 1 | `F(1)`, and `F(5, 6)` with no `As` | 13 |
| `Function F() As Variant`, returning a 2-D array with `m(1, 0) = 7` | `F(1, 0)` | Integer 7 |
| `Function F() As Collection` | `F(1)` | the Item |
| `Function F() As Long`, `As String`, `As Long()` | `F(1)` | compile error, "Wrong number of arguments or invalid property assignment" |
| `Function Opt(Optional n As Integer = 0)` returning `Array(n, n + 1)` | `Opt(1)`, `Opt(1)(1)`, `Opt()(1)` | the array for 1, then 2, then 1: an Optional parameter takes the argument |
| `NoArgs` as above | `NoArgs(1)(0)`, `NoArgs(5)` | 13, 9 |

So a parameterless procedure that returns a Variant or an object reads its arguments as an index into its result, and
`F(1)` is `F()(1)`. A class's method and Property Get do the same: `k.Items(2)`, `k.Prop(1)`, `k.Bag(1)`. A typed
return does not compile, even a typed array. #741's table had `Function F(): F = 1`, then `F(5, 6)`, as "Expected
array" at compile time; in this shape it compiles and raises 13, which agrees with its TE_04 row. Both rows stand.

### Writing

| statement | vb6.exe |
|---|---|
| `a(1)(0) = 9`, with `a = Array(Array(1, 2), Array(3, 4))` | `a(1)(0)` is 9: written through to the inner array |
| `v = a(1): v(1) = 99` | `a(1)(1)` is still 4: `v` holds a copy |
| `V3()(1) = 5` and `NoArgs()(1) = 7` | compile, run the Function, and change nothing else |

### What does not compile

| expression | compile error |
|---|---|
| `Scalar()(0)`, with `Scalar() As Integer` | Type mismatch |
| `Left$("abc", 2)(0)` | Type mismatch |
| `Len("abc")(0)` | **Syntax error** |
| `a(0)(1) = 5`, with `Dim a(1) As Integer` | Type mismatch |

### The order of evaluation

Each argument and subscript was a call that logged a tag.

| expression | order logged |
|---|---|
| `F3(a1, a2, a3)` | a1, a2, a3, then the body |
| `F3(a1, a2, a3)(i)` | a1, a2, **i**, a3, body |
| `F2(a1, a2)(i1)(i2)` | a1, **i2, i1**, a2, body |
| `F1(a1)(i1)(i2)` | **i2, i1**, a1, body |
| `G2(a1, a2)(i1, i2)` | a1, **i1, i2**, a2, body |
| `TwoArgs(a1, a2)(i)` | a1, i, a2 |
| `Jag(...)(i1)(i2)(i3)` | i3, i2, i1, then the body |
| `Split(t)(i)` | **i, t** |
| `Split(s, d)(i)` | **s, d, i** |
| `arr(i1, i2)`, read | i1, i2 |
| `arr(i1, i2) = rhs` | rhs, i1, i2 |
| `a(i1)(i2)(i3)`, read | i3, i2, i1 |
| `a(w1)(w2) = rhs` | w2, rhs, w1 |
| `a(w1)(w2)(w3) = rhs` | w3, rhs, w2, w1 |

The rule for a Function's call and an array's element: all but the last of the first group's arguments or subscripts,
left to right; then the later groups, the last group first, each left to right; then the first group's last; then the
call. The read of `a(i1)(i2)(i3)` follows it, its first group being `(i1)`.

**A library function does not follow it, and no rule I would defend covers both rows.** `Split(t)(i)` evaluates the
index first, as the rule says. `Split(s, d)(i)` evaluates both arguments first, where the rule says s, i, d. Two rows
were measured, nothing more.

**A chain's Let** evaluates its last group, then the value, then the other groups from the last, then the first. A plain
`arr(i1, i2) = rhs` evaluates the value first.

### In HexIDE (#1476)

- **The groups.** `ExpressionExecutor.ParenGroups` gives each parenthesised group, an empty `()` as a group of its own.
  The grammar gives an argsCall only to a group with something in it, so `T3()(1)` used to read as `T3(1)`.
- **Reading.** `EvaluateProcedureOrArrayCall` evaluates the later groups through `LaterGroups`. The argument loops call it
  before their last argument (`ResolveCallArgs`, `EvaluateCallArgs`), which is the rule above. A library function calls
  it before one argument and after two, as the two Split rows did, and that is no more than those two rows.
  `IndexResult` then indexes, as the reading table says.
- **Member chains.** A member segment's later groups go the same way (`ResolveMemberIndexed`). They used to be dropped
  together with the first, so `k.Echo("m n")(1)` called Echo with no arguments.
- **Parameterless procedures.** `IndexesItsResult` makes one returning a Variant or an object, given arguments, a call
  with none and an index. A typed return given arguments is #741's.
- **Writing.** `StatementExecutor.LetIntoIndexChain` writes in the Let order above. `Len("abc")(0)` is "Type mismatch"
  here, a different message for a program both refuse.

## What VB6's Add Form saves (2026-10-23, #1532, design-time, IDE, release build)

**The question.** A form HexIDE created started with an empty `Private Sub Form_Load()` / `End Sub`, written to the
file at its first save. #1369 had already matched the rest of the file to VB6's template `Form1.frm`, which has no
code, but nobody had looked at what VB6's own Add Form writes.

**The probe.** VB6.EXE 6.00.8176, the IDE, in the guest's console session, driven with SendKeys and a screenshot at
each step. `probe.vbp` is a Standard EXE holding `Module1.bas` alone (`Sub Main`). Opened in the IDE, then Project >
Add Form, which showed the Add Form dialog on its New tab with Form selected; Enter. Then Ctrl+S, which showed Save File
As with `Form1` in the project's folder; Enter. VB6 was then stopped, without saving the project, and the file read
back.

**What it wrote**, 485 bytes, every line CRLF:

```
VERSION 5.00
Begin VB.Form Form1 
   Caption         =   "Form1"
   ClientHeight    =   3015
   ClientLeft      =   120
   ClientTop       =   465
   ClientWidth     =   4560
   LinkTopic       =   "Form1"
   ScaleHeight     =   3015
   ScaleWidth      =   4560
   StartUpPosition =   3  'Windows Default
End
Attribute VB_Name = "Form1"
Attribute VB_GlobalNameSpace = False
Attribute VB_Creatable = False
Attribute VB_PredeclaredId = True
Attribute VB_Exposed = False
```

The last bytes are `... 46 61 6C 73 65 0D 0A`: the file ends at `Attribute VB_Exposed = False` and its line break.

**What it shows:**
- **A new form has no code.** VB6 adds an event procedure when the developer asks for one, by double-clicking the form
  or picking it in the Procedure box. HexIDE's seed `Form_Load` was its own invention.
- **The designer block differs from HexIDE's in more than the code.** VB6's toolbar read the form as 4800 × 3600
  outside. Its client area, 4560 × 3015, and its `ClientLeft` 120 and `ClientTop` 465, are that outer size less the
  borders and caption of this guest's theme, so those numbers are this machine's, not constants. `LinkTopic = "Form1"`
  is written too. HexIDE's new form has a client area of 6000 × 4500 and writes neither `ClientLeft`, `ClientTop` nor
  `LinkTopic`. That is #1538.

**A double-click on the form.** With the new form gone empty, a double-click is how it gets its `Form_Load`, so that
was measured too. Same rig: the project opened, Ctrl+R, the form, Shift+F7 for its designer, a real double-click of the
mouse inside it, then Ctrl+S at once, with nothing typed. Two forms, each the file above plus a code section:

| Form's code before | What follows `Attribute VB_Exposed = False` after the save |
|---|---|
| none | `Private Sub Form_Load()` CRLF, CRLF, `End Sub` CRLF |
| `Option Explicit`, a blank line, `Private Sub Zeta()` … `End Sub` | that code, then CRLF, `Private Sub Form_Load()` CRLF, CRLF, `End Sub` CRLF |

- **The procedure is `Private`, CRLF, with one blank line inside**, and the caret on that line (the code window read Ln 8,
  Col 1 in the second row).
- **It goes at the end**, one blank line below the code, not sorted among the procedures. Below a header with no code,
  there is no blank line.
- **An empty procedure is kept.** Saved at once, with nothing typed, it is written.

HexIDE's double-click wrote `Public Sub Form_Load()` in bare LF, after two bare line feeds, into a CRLF file. That had
been hidden, because a new form already had its seeded `Form_Load` to navigate to. An event picked in the Procedure box
was `Private` already, but ended at `End Sub` with no line break, its line breaks the host's, and its caret after `End Sub`.

**In HexIDE (#1532):** the `FormDefinition` constructor's seed is now empty, so a form HexIDE creates is written ending at
its `Attribute` block, as VB6's is. Both ways of adding an event procedure now write it as the table shows: `Private`, in
the file's line breaks, at the end, one blank line below any code, with the caret on the blank line inside.

**Add User Control and Add Property Page** (#1538). The same rig, with the Project menu's Add User Control (`u`) and
Add Property Page (`p`), Enter on the dialog's default, then Ctrl+S and Enter. Each file ends at
`Attribute VB_Exposed = False` and its CRLF, with no code:

| | UserControl1.ctl | PropertyPage1.pag |
|---|---|---|
| `Caption` | none | `"PropertyPage1"` |
| `ClientHeight` × `ClientWidth` | 3600 × 4800 | 3600 × 4800 |
| `ClientLeft`, `ClientTop` | 0, 0 | 0, 0 |
| other properties | none | `PaletteMode = 0 'Halftone` |
| `VB_Creatable` | **True** | False |
| `VB_PredeclaredId` | **False** | False |
| `VB_GlobalNameSpace`, `VB_Exposed` | False, False | False, False |

- **Neither has a border**, so its client area is VB6's 4800 × 3600 window itself, at 0, 0. These are constants, where a
  form's are its machine's.
- **A UserControl has no `Caption`.** HexIDE's had one, from the form constructor it shared.
- **The `Attribute` block is not a form's.** A UserControl is creatable and neither has a default instance. HexIDE wrote
  `VB_Name` alone for both.
- Not measured: an ActiveX Control project, where `VB_Exposed` may be True.

**In HexIDE (#1538):** `FormDefinition.NewForm` takes VB6's 4560 × 3015 client area at 120, 465, and its `LinkTopic`, which
HexIDE does not model and keeps as a loaded form's raw line. `ModuleDefinition.NewDesigner` makes a new UserControl or
PropertyPage as the table shows, its `PaletteMode` kept the same way. Each new file is now VB6's byte for byte.

## Write # and Input # (2026-10-23, #1521)

Measured with `/make` in ten batches, native and p-code identical on every row. All of them are run-time results of
built EXEs on SP6's MSVBVM60 (#1524), and none is a compile error. The guest's locale was en-GB, except for one batch run
under de-DE: the culture was switched with `Set-Culture`, then restored and checked from a fresh session. A written file
was read back byte by byte with Binary `Get`. A file `Input #` read was written first with `Print #f, text;`. Each typed
variable was set to a known value first, so that an error could be told from a store.

### What Write # writes

| statement | bytes written |
|---|---|
| `Write #f, 5, -5, 0, 32767, 70000` | `5,-5,0,32767,70000` CR LF |
| `Write #f, 2.5, -2.5, 0.5, -0.5, 1E+20, 1.5E-07` | `2.5,-2.5,.5,-.5,1E+20,.00000015` |
| `Write #f, CSng(0.1), CDbl(0.1), CCur(2.5), CCur(-0.25), CDec(1.5), CByte(7)` | `.1,.1,2.5,-.25,1.5,7` |
| `Write #f, 1E-10, 1.5E-20, -1E-05, 0.0001, 0.00001` | `.0000000001,1.5E-20,-.00001,.0001,.00001` |
| `Write #f, 1E-15, 1E-16, 1.5E-14, 1.5E-15, 1.25E-14, 0.000123456789012345` | `.000000000000001,1E-16,.000000000000015,1.5E-15,1.25E-14,1.23456789012345E-04` |
| `Write #f, 1E+15, 1E+16, 1.23456789012345E+15, 123456789012345#, 12345.6789` | `1E+15,1E+16,1.23456789012345E+15,123456789012345,12345.6789` |
| `Write #f, 999999999999999#, 1E+15 - 1, 1234567890123456#, -1E-15, -1E+15` | `999999999999999,999999999999999,1.23456789012346E+15,-.000000000000001,-1E+15` |
| `Write #f, CSng(1 / 3), CDbl(1 / 3), 0.1 + 0.2, CSng(1E+20), CSng(1E-10)` | `.3333333,.333333333333333,.3,1E+20,1E-10` |
| `Write #f, CSng(1.5E-06), CSng(1.5E-07), CSng(1234567), CSng(12345678), CSng(0.0000001), CSng(0.000001)` | `.0000015,1.5E-07,1234567,1.234568E+07,.0000001,.000001` |
| `Write #f, CCur("922337203685477.5807"), CCur("-0.0001"), CCur(100)` | `922337203685477.5807,-.0001,100` |
| `Write #f, CDec("79228162514264337593543950335"), CDec("0.0000000000000000000000000001"), CDec("1E+20"), CDec(-0.5)` | `79228162514264337593543950335,.0000000000000000000000000001,100000000000000000000,-.5` |
| `Write #f, "a", "", "b c", "x,y", " lead"` | `"a","","b c","x,y"," lead"` |
| `Write #f, "say ""hi"""` and `Write #f, "a""b", "c"` | `"say ""hi"""` and `"a""b","c"`: an inner quote is doubled |
| `Write #f, True, False` | `#TRUE#,#FALSE#` |
| `Write #f, #1/2/2003#, #1/2/2003 1:45:00 PM#, #1:45:00 PM#, #12/30/1899#` | `#2003-01-02#,#2003-01-02 13:45:00#,#1899-12-30 13:45:00#,#1899-12-30#` |
| `Write #f, #1/1/1800#, #1/1/100#, #12/31/9999 11:59:59 PM#, CDate(-1.5), CDate(0.5), #1/2/2003 12:00:00 AM#` | `#1800-01-01#,#0100-01-01#,#9999-12-31 23:59:59#,#1899-12-29 12:00:00#,#1899-12-30 12:00:00#,#2003-01-02#` |
| `Write #f, v, w, "end"`, with `v` Null and `w` Empty | `#NULL#,,"end"` |
| `Write #f, CVErr(5)` in a Variant | `#ERROR 5#` |
| `Write #f, "a"; "b"; 5` | `"a","b",5`: a `;` writes a comma as `,` does |
| `Write #f, "a",` and `Write #f, "a";` | `"a",` and no line break |
| `Write #f, "a";`, then `Write #f, "b"` | `"a","b"` CR LF: the next Write goes on with no further comma |
| `Write #f,` | CR LF |
| `Write #f, "l1" & vbCrLf & "l2", 1` | `"l1` CR LF `l2",1`: a line break in a string is written as it is |
| `Write #f, "a", Spc(2), "b"` and `Write #f, "a", Tab(6), "b"` | `"a",  ,"b"` and `"a", ,"b"` |
| `Write #f, ChrW(&H100) & ChrW(&H416), ChrW(&H141)` | `"A?","L"`: best fit, as `Print #` (#1511) |

**How a number is written.** No leading zero, and a point whatever the locale. A Double is fixed while the fixed form needs
at most 15 digits, counting the whole part's digits, or a fraction's with its leading zeros. Otherwise it is written as
`1.5E-20`: its significant digits, `E`, a sign, and at least two exponent digits. A Single is the same at 7 digits.
Currency and Decimal are always fixed: `CDec("1E+20")` is 21 digits. So `1E-10` is `.0000000001` as a Double but `1E-10` as
a Single. Write # does not write as `Str` or `CStr` do.

**A date** is `#yyyy-mm-dd#`, with ` hh:mm:ss` after it where the time is not midnight. A time alone is written on the zero
date, never by itself.

### Under de-DE

| | de-DE |
|---|---|
| `CStr(2.5)` and `Str(2.5)` | `2,5` and ` 2.5` |
| `Write #f, 2.5, -0.25, 1E+20, CCur(2.5), CDec(1.5), CSng(0.1), #1/2/2003#, True` | `2.5,-.25,1E+20,2.5,1.5,.1,#2003-01-02#,#TRUE#` |
| `Print #f, 2.5; CCur(2.5)` | ` 2,5  2,5 `: Print # follows the locale |
| `Input #` of `2.5,"1,5",2.12345` into Variants | Currency 2,5, String 1,5, Decimal 2,12345 |
| `Input #` of `2.5` into a Double | 2,5, so the point read as a point |
| `Input #` of `"2,5"` into a Double | 0 |

Neither statement follows the locale.

### How Input # reads a field

- **Blanks** (spaces and tabs) before a field are skipped.
- **Where a field ends.** A field ends at a comma or a CR, which it takes with it, CR LF as one. A lone LF is an ordinary
  character: `1` LF `2` CR `3` into three Variants is 1, 3, then 62, and `a` LF `b,c` into Strings is `a` LF `b`, then `c`.
- **After a quoted field, a `#` form or a number**, blanks are skipped and a comma or line end is taken. Anything else
  begins the next field: `"a" junk,b` is a, junk, b; `"a""b","c"` is a, b, c; `5 x,6` is 5, x, 6; `5 ,6` is 5, 6.
- **A quoted field** runs to the next quote, or to the end of the file, line breaks included: `"open` CR LF is
  `open` CR LF, with no error. So a doubled quote ends it. **What Write # writes for a string holding a quote does not
  read back**: `"say ""hi"""` reads as `say `.
- **The line end after a line's last field is taken too.** So `Input #f, n` of `3` CR LF `line1` leaves `Line Input #`
  `line1`. After a comma it is not: `8,` CR LF `line` leaves `Line Input #` an empty line, and `5,6` leaves it `6`.

**What a field is read as depends on the variable:**

- **A numeric variable** (Byte, Integer, Long, Single, Double, Currency) reads every field as a number, which a blank,
  comma or CR ends. Quotes and `#` count as characters, not as delimiters: `#ERROR 5#,#abc#` into two Integers is 0 and 5,
  and `a b,5` is 0 and 0.
- **A String** reads a quoted field, or else the text to the comma or CR, with trailing blanks dropped: `1 2,3` is `1 2`,
  `12abc,5` is `12abc`, and ` a ` is `a`.
- **A Variant, a Boolean or a Date** go by the first character. A quote begins a quoted field and `#` a `#` form, which runs
  to the closing `#`, or else to the comma: `#,5` is `#`, then 5. A digit, sign, point or `&` begins a number, which a blank
  ends, so `1 2` is two fields. Anything else is text to the comma: `hello world`.

### What a Variant becomes

| field | Variant |
|---|---|
| `5`, `-5`, `-0`, `+5`, `5.`, `1.00000`, `5.0` | Integer |
| `70000`, `32768`, `2147483647` | Long |
| `2147483648`, `123456789012`, `922337203685477`, `999999999999999` | Double: a whole number beyond Long with at most 15 digits |
| `1234567890123456`, `9999999999999999`, `100000000000000000000`, `12345678901234567890` | Decimal: 16 to 29 digits |
| `123456789012345678901234567890` | Double 1.23456789012346E+29: past Decimal |
| `2.5`, `.5`, `-1.5`, `1.50`, `2.10000`, `0.12340`, `1.2345`, `99999.9999`, `123456789012.5`, `922337203685477.5807` | Currency: at most 4 places once trailing zeros are dropped |
| `2.12345`, `1.23456`, `-.00001`, `.00000015`, `1234567890123456.5` | Decimal: more places, or past Currency |
| `1.123456789012345678901234567890` | Decimal 1.1234567890123456789012345679, rounded to 29 digits |
| `.000000000000000000000000000012` | Double 1.2E-29: still more than 28 places after rounding |
| `0.0`, `0.0000` | Currency 0 |
| `0.00000`, `-0.00000` | Decimal 0 |
| `1e3`, `1d3`, `1E+20`, `1E+300` | Double |
| `1E-400` | Double 0 |
| `1E+400` | String `1E+400`: too large for a Double |
| `&H10`, `&O17`, `&HFFFF`, `&H8000`, `&O177777` | Integer 16, 15, -1, -32768, -1 |
| `&H10000`, `&H7FFFFFFF` | Long |
| `&HFFFFFFFF`, `&H1FFFFFFFF` | Integer -1: 32 bits, higher ones dropped, then 16 where it fits |
| `12abc`, `5%` | Integer 12 and 5: what follows the number is dropped, to the comma |
| `-abc`, `.`, `-&H10`, `(5)`, `abc`, `TRUE` | String, as written |
| `#TRUE#`, `#FALSE#`, `#NULL#`, `#ERROR 13#` | Boolean, Boolean, Null, Error 13 |
| `#2003-01-02#`, `#2003-01-02 13:45:00#`, `#13:45:00#`, `#1/2/2003#` | Date. Inside `#`s the month comes first, as in a date literal: `#1/2/2003#` is 2 January |
| `#abc#`, `#` | String, as written |
| `""` | String, empty |
| nothing before the comma, or only blanks | Empty |

**Measured, but no rule I would defend:** `0.00000` and `-0.00000` are Decimal 0, where `1.00000` is an Integer 1 and
`0.0000` a Currency 0. The table holds if zero keeps the places it was written with, while trailing zeros after any
other digit are dropped. That reading fits all these rows, and nothing more was probed.

### What a typed variable becomes

| variable | field | result |
|---|---|---|
| Integer | `2.5`, `3.5`, `2.5"` | 2, 4, 2: rounded half to even, as a Let rounds |
| Integer | `abc`, `"5"`, `""`, `#TRUE#`, `#NULL#`, `-`, nothing | 0, no error |
| Integer | `1E3`, `&HFFFF` | 1000, -1 |
| Integer | `70000`, `-32769`, `1E+309` | 6, and the variable keeps what it had |
| Long | `1E3`; `2147483648`; `"5"` | 1000; 6; 0 |
| Byte | `255`; `300`, `-1`; `"5"` | 255; 6; 0 |
| Single | `0.1`, `1.5E-07`; `1E+39`; `"2.5"` | 0.1, 1.5E-07; 6; 0 |
| Double | `2.5`, `1E3`, `.5`, `5`; `1,5` | 2.5, 1000, 0.5, 5; 1 |
| Double | `abc`, `"5"`, `"2.5"`, `""`, `#TRUE#`, `#2003-01-02#`, `#2.5#`, `x2.5`, `-` | 0, no error |
| Double | `1E+309`, `1E+400` | 6, kept |
| Currency | `2.12345`; `abc`, `"5"`; `1E+309` | 2.1234; 0; 6 |
| String | `""`, ` a `, `5`, `#2003-01-02#`, `#NULL#`, `#TRUE#`, `#ERROR 5#` | empty, `a`, `5`, and each `#` form as written |
| Boolean | `#TRUE#`, `#FALSE#` | True, False |
| Boolean | `True`, `abc`, `"True"`, `""`, nothing | False, no error |
| Boolean | `1`, `0`, `-1`, `2` | 6, kept: a number in any form |
| Boolean | `#NULL#`, `#2003-01-02#` | 13, kept |
| Date | `#2003-01-02#`, `#13:45:00#` | the date, the time |
| Date | `abc`, `"2003-01-02"`, `"abc"`, `""`, nothing | the zero date, no error |
| Date | `2003-01-02`, `02/01/2003`, `37000` | 6, kept: each begins with a number |
| Date | `#NULL#`, `#TRUE#` | 13, kept |

A Boolean or a Date takes the field as a Variant would, and then:
- a String or Empty is False, or the zero date;
- a number is 6;
- a Boolean or a Date of the other kind, or Null, is 13.

A numeric variable reads 0 from anything with no number at its start, a quoted field included, so `Write #` of a String
holding `"5"` reads back into an Integer as 0.

### At the end of the file

- **A Variant** is emptied, then the statement raises 62. That holds for one that held `"kept"`, whether the file was
  empty or `1` CR LF had already been read, and for the third of three Variants reading `1,2`.
- **A typed variable** keeps what it had, and the statement raises 62: Integer, String, Date and Boolean were measured.

### In HexIDE (#1521)

- `VbWrite.ItemText` formats a value. `VisitWriteStmt` writes a comma for each separator, and moves for `Spc` and `Tab` as
  `Print #` does.
- `VbFiles.ReadField` reads a field as `InputReading` says, from the variable's type.
- `VbInput` converts the field. Its number reader is its own, invariant and decimal-exact, and is not `CDbl`'s
  locale-aware one (#1047).

Refused, untrappably and by name:
- `Input #` into anything but a plain variable, as `Line Input #` refuses;
- `#ERROR n#` into a Variant, since HexIDE has no Error values (`CVErr`);
- `Write #` of an object, array or user-defined type, which was not measured.
- a date between `#`s in any shape but the four measured (`#yyyy-mm-dd#`, `#yyyy-mm-dd hh:mm:ss#`, `#hh:mm:ss#`,
  `#m/d/yyyy#`). .NET's lenient parser would read `#1/2#` as this year's 2 January. A form no date parser takes stays
  the String as written, as `#abc#` measured.

## Make Project Group (2026-10-23, #746, design-time, IDE, release build)

**The question.** With one project loaded, HexIDE's File > Make Project Group threw on the missing group, and nothing
said so. The issue asked whether VB6 offers the command with one project. Reading the code raised a second question:
what the command does. HexIDE's saves every project and the group file.

**The probe.** Two projects, each with an empty form, plus `group.vbg` naming both and `single.vbg` naming only the
first. Each was opened in VB6's IDE, and I read the File menu. Where the command was offered, I chose it, then pressed
Cancel. The folder's file times were read before and after.

| Opened | Make Project Group... | Choosing it |
|---|---|---|
| `probe1.vbp` alone | **greyed** | |
| `group.vbg` (two projects) | enabled | a dialog: "Build the following projects:", listing `probe1.vbp` and `probe2.vbp`, both selected; "Use Default Build Options", ticked; Build, Cancel, Help |
| `single.vbg` (one project) | **enabled** | the same dialog, listing `probe1.vbp` alone |

**What it shows:**
- **The command needs a group open, not two projects.** A group of one project offers it; one project without a group
  doesn't. The File menu reflects the same state: Save Project Group and Save Project Group As replace Save Project
  and Save Project As whenever a group is open, one project or two.
- **It builds.** It's the group's counterpart of Make *project*.exe, not a save. Opening the dialog and cancelling
  wrote nothing: every file kept its time.

**In HexIDE (#746):**
- The command is offered only with a group open, or with two projects loaded. HexIDE's implicit Group1 can lag
  behind a second project, so two projects count as a group. With one project and no group it is greyed out.
- With a group, it says the feature isn't implemented yet and writes nothing, because HexIDE can't build a group
  (#1515). It used to save every project and the group, which is Save Project Group's job, under a Make label.

**Not measured:**
- What Build writes, ticked or unticked "Use Default Build Options", and whether it saves anything first (#1515).
- What VB6 does to a group when a project is removed from it. HexIDE drops its group at one project.

## How a running form stacks its controls (2026-10-23, #1497, IDE, release build)

**The question.** "Where VB6's designer puts a control's block" measured windowed controls at run time, and the
windowless plane only in the designer. It left three things open:
- a windowless control written *before* a windowed one;
- a Line or a Shape beside a Label;
- where a control-array element loaded at run time goes.

**The probe.** A form, written by hand so that each pair overlaps and the first-named control comes first in the
file:

| Pair, in file order | Designer | Run time (F5) |
|---|---|---|
| LabelA (red), then CommandA | the button over the Label | the same |
| LabelB (yellow), then LineB (blue, 8 wide) | the Label over the Line; the Line shows only past the Label's ends | the same |
| LineC, then LabelC | the Line over the Label | the same |
| ShapeD (solid green), then LabelD (yellow) | the Shape over the Label | the same |
| LabelE, then ShapeE | the Label over the Shape | the same |
| CommandF, then CmdArr(0); `Form_Load` loads CmdArr(1) and moves it over both | | CmdArr(1) is under both |

**What it shows:**
- **A windowless control is drawn under a windowed one even when its block comes first.** VB6 never writes a
  file that way, so only a hand-written file shows it.
- **Among the windowless controls, the first block is on top, whatever the class.** A Label covers a Line or
  a Shape written after it, and is covered by one written before it.
- **A control-array element loaded at run time goes under every windowed control already there.** That covers its
  own array's elements and other controls alike. The designer puts a new control on top, so `Load` does the
  opposite.
- **Design time and run time agree on every pair.**

**In HexIDE (#1497):**
- **The running form stacks by these rules.** Each control placed on a container goes under every control of its
  plane already there. Placing a form's controls in file order therefore puts the first on top, and a `Load`ed
  element at the bottom.
- **Lines in the designer** are stacked like any other windowless control. They used to go under every other control,
  Labels included, and so under a Frame holding one.
- **Not done:** the `ZOrder` method is still not implemented, and a program calling it stops (#1503, since done: "What
  ZOrder does at run time").

**Not measured:**
- An Image beside a Label.
- A windowless element loaded at run time. HexIDE puts it at the bottom of the windowless plane, by the same rule.
- `ZOrder` at run time.

## Too few arguments to an intrinsic (2026-10-23, #1512)

Measured with `/make`, one project per call since the compile error stops the build, native and p-code agreeing on every
row. Each call was `x = <call>` with `x` a Variant. Eleven rows were measured separately with `scripts/vb6-oracle.ps1`,
and agree wherever the two overlap.

A compile error is the compiler's answer, not the runtime's. So these rows come from the oracle's VB6.EXE 6.00.8176 and
VBA6.DLL 6.0.8169, the release build, even though built EXEs run on SP6's MSVBVM60 (#1524). Re-measure them once SP6 is
installed.

**"Syntax error":**

| calls | |
|---|---|
| `Abs()`, `Int()`, `Fix()`, `Sgn()` | the arithmetic intrinsics |
| `CBool()`, `CByte()`, `CCur()`, `CDate()`, `CDbl()`, `CInt()`, `CLng()`, `CSng()`, `CStr()`, `CVar()`, `CVErr()` | every conversion but `CDec` and `CVDate` |
| `Len()`, `LenB()`, `LBound()`, `UBound()` | |
| `InStr("a")`, `StrComp("a")` | one argument of two |
| `String()`, `String(3)` | none, and one of two |

**"Argument not optional":**

| calls | |
|---|---|
| `CDec()`, `CVDate()` | the two conversions outside the first set |
| `Chr()`, `Chr$()`, `ChrW()`, `Asc()`, `AscW()`, `Hex()`, `Oct()`, `Str()`, `Val()` | |
| `LCase()`, `UCase()`, `Trim()`, `Space()`, `Round()` | |
| `IsNull()`, `TypeName()`, `VarType()`, `Format()`, `Split()`, `Join()` | |
| `Mid("a")`, `Mid$("a")`, `Left("a")`, `Right("a")`, `Mid("abc", , 2)` | the length, or the start, left out |
| `Replace("a", "b")`, `IIf(True, 1)`, `DateAdd("d", 1)` | one argument short |

**Too many:** `Chr(65, 66)` is "Wrong number of arguments or invalid property assignment".

**None needed:** `Array()` compiles, and gives an empty `Variant()`.

**Comparing it with the named-argument rule.** The "Syntax error" set is the set that refuses a named argument with
"Syntax error" (#1465, `TakesNoNamedArguments`), name for name, with two differences:
- `String` takes its names, `Number` and `Character`, yet is "Syntax error" short of an argument, which
  `OmittedIsSyntaxError` already records.
- `LenB`'s named-argument row is unmeasured.

`CDec` and `CVDate` take names, and fall with the rest. This is a measured correlation across these 53 calls, not a rule
VB6 documents, so an intrinsic outside the table should be measured, not inferred.

### In HexIDE

Unchanged here: a call with too few arguments still fails as #1512 describes. These rows are what that fix pins.

## Print # and the ANSI best fit (2026-10-23, #1511)

Measured on vb6.exe under code page 1252, native and p-code identical. Each file was read back byte by byte with `Get`
in Binary mode.

| statement | bytes written |
|---|---|
| `Print #f, ChrW(&H100) & ChrW(&H416) & ChrW(&H2019) & ChrW(&H141) & ChrW(&H3B1) & ChrW(&H20AC);` | `41 3F 92 4C 61 80` |
| `Write #f, ChrW(&H100) & ChrW(&H416), ChrW(&H141)` | `22 41 3F 22 2C 22 4C 22 0D 0A` |
| `Print #f, ChrW(&H100);`, to a file opened For Append | `41` |

Taking the characters in turn:
- **Best fits:** Ā is "A", Ł is "L", and Greek α is "a".
- **No fit:** Ж is "?".
- **1252's own bytes:** ’ is 92 and € is 80.

`Write #` best-fits inside its quotes as `Print #` does, and Append as Output does. This is the table the clipboard
section above measured (U+0100 to A, U+0416 to ?), and the one `Asc` uses (#1134): Windows' own conversion to the ANSI
code page, not a `?` for every character the code page lacks.

### In HexIDE (#1511)

`VbFiles.Ansi()` is the code page's own encoding, cloned so that only its decoder fallback is replaced. Its encoder keeps
the table's best fit. Before, both directions had a `?` replacement, so every character 1252 lacked was written as `?`.
`Line Input #` reads as before. `Write #` is not implemented yet ([#1521](https://github.com/hexide-io/HexIDE/issues/1521)), so only its measurement is recorded.

## CVar (2026-10-23, #1466)

Measured on vb6.exe, native and p-code identical, under en-GB. Each program `CVarTests` pins was made as written.

**CVar returns its argument as a Variant, with the argument's own type.** It converts nothing.

| probe | result |
|---|---|
| `TypeName(CVar(5))`, `CVar("5")`, `CVar(Null)`, `CVar(Empty)` | Integer, String, Null, Empty |
| `TypeName(CVar(n))`, `n As Integer` | Integer |
| `TypeName(CVar(2.5))`, `CVar(70000)`, `CVar(True)`, `CVar(#1/2/2000#)` | Double, Long, Boolean, Date |
| `TypeName(CVar(a))`, `a(1) As Integer` | `Integer()`: the typed array, not a Variant array |
| `TypeName(CVar(Array(1, 2)))` | `Variant()` |
| `TypeName(CVar(c))`, `c` a Collection | Collection: the object itself |
| `TypeName(CVar(k))`, `k` a class with a default `Value` of 7 | K1, and `IsObject(CVar(k))` True: the object, not its default member. `CVar(k) + 1` is 8 and `VarType(CVar(k))` 2, both of which read the default member |
| `TypeName(CVar(Nothing))` | Nothing |
| `v = CVar(a)`, then `v(0) = 9` | `a(0)` is still 1: the Variant holds a copy |

**The result reads as a Variant's** (#987's probe):
- `CVar(5) * 7000` and `CVar(n) * 7000` are a Long 35000, where `5 * 7000` is 6.
- `CVar(5)` against `Case Is < 5.4` takes the Case.
- `CVar("9")` against `Case Is > 10` takes Case Else, read as 9.
- `CVar("5") + 1` is a Double 6, and `CVar("abc") + 1` is 13.

**Two compile-time surprises:**
- **`CVar$` compiles, and ignores the `$`.** `TypeName(CVar$(5))` is Integer and `CVar$("9")` takes Case Else, as `CVar` does. `CVar$(Null)` is Null, not 94, so it does not behave as the `$` forms that answer a String do.
- **`CVar()` is "Syntax error", not "Argument not optional"** (HexIDE: #1512). `CVar(Expression:=5)` is "Syntax error" too (#1465).

### In HexIDE (#1466)

`d["CVar"]` returns its argument unchanged. It is listed:
- in `ExpressionExecutor.VariantIntrinsics`, so the result reads as a Variant's;
- in `DollarIgnored`, for `CVar$`;
- in `VB6BuiltIns.TakesTheArgumentItself`, so an object reaches it as the object, as it reaches `TypeName`.

A copy of an array is made where the result is stored, as for any Let of an array (#970).

## Filesystem (#1561) — vb6.exe 6.00.8176 (original release), MSVBVM60 6.00.9848 (SP6-level)

All rows are run-time results of `/make` EXEs (#1524).

**Native and p-code agree on every row**, so each one below holds for both. Every row is a run-time result from a compiled EXE run in session 0 in the oracle guest, on NTFS. Each operation ran under `On Error Resume Next`, and its `Err.Number` and `Err.Description` were logged.

### The fixture

The probe made `App.Path\fx` itself with `MkDir`. Inside it:
- `a.txt` holds 3 bytes and `b.txt` 2. The other files hold a byte or two each: `c.htm`, `d.html`, `x.tmp`, `y.tmp`.
- `h.txt` is set `vbHidden`, `r.txt` `vbReadOnly` and `s.txt` `vbSystem`.
- The directories are `sub`, which holds `in.txt`, and `empty`.

A file "open" below means open in the same program.

### CurDir

| Call | Result |
|---|---|
| `CurDir` | String, equal to `App.Path` (the process's working directory). `CurDir$` is String too |
| `CurDir("C")`, `CurDir("c")`, `CurDir("C:\Windows")` | `C:\…`: only the first character counts, in either case |
| `CurDir("")` | the same as `CurDir` |
| `CurDir("Q")`, a drive that doesn't exist | **68** Device unavailable |
| `CurDir("1")` | **5** Invalid procedure call or argument |

### MkDir and RmDir

| Call | Result |
|---|---|
| `MkDir` a new directory | made |
| `MkDir base & "\slash\"`, with a trailing backslash | made |
| `MkDir` an existing directory | **75** Path/File access error |
| `MkDir` onto an existing file | **75** |
| `MkDir` with a missing parent | **76** Path not found. No intermediate directories are made |
| `MkDir ""` | **76** |
| `RmDir` an empty directory | removed |
| `RmDir` a directory that isn't empty | **75** |
| `RmDir` a missing directory | **76** |
| `RmDir` a file | **76** |
| `RmDir base & "\w*"`, with a wildcard | **76**, and the directory survives |
| `RmDir ""` | **76** |

### FileLen, FileDateTime and GetAttr

| Call | Result |
|---|---|
| `FileLen("a.txt")` | Long 3 |
| `FileLen` of a hidden file | Long 1: hidden files are not skipped |
| `FileLen` of a directory | Long 0 |
| `FileLen` of a missing file, or of `""` | **53** File not found |
| `FileLen` with a wildcard | **52** Bad file name or number |
| `FileLen` of a file open for Output with 5 bytes `Print`ed, before `Close` | Long **0**: what is on disk, not what is buffered |
| … after `Close` | Long 5 |
| `FileDateTime(file)` | **Date**, whole seconds, today's date |
| `FileDateTime` of a directory | Date |
| `FileDateTime` of a missing file | **53** |
| `FileDateTime` with a wildcard | **52** |
| `GetAttr` of a normal file just written | Long **32** (`vbArchive`) |
| `GetAttr` of a directory | Long 16 |
| `GetAttr` of `sub\`, with a trailing backslash | Long 16 |
| `GetAttr` of hidden, read-only and system files | Long 2, 1 and 4. `SetAttr` replaces the whole set, so Archive is gone |
| `GetAttr("C:\")` | Long 22 (Directory, System and Hidden) |
| `GetAttr` of a missing file, or of `""` | **53** |
| `GetAttr` with a wildcard | **52** |

### SetAttr

| Call | Result |
|---|---|
| `SetAttr f, vbNormal`, then `GetAttr` | 0 |
| `vbArchive` | 32 |
| `vbReadOnly Or vbHidden Or vbSystem Or vbArchive` | 39 |
| `SetAttr` back to `vbNormal` | 0 |
| `SetAttr f, vbDirectory` or `vbVolume` | **5** |
| `SetAttr` a directory to `vbHidden` | `GetAttr` gives 18: the Directory bit is kept |
| … then to `vbNormal` | 16 |
| `SetAttr` a missing file | **53** |
| `SetAttr` with a wildcard | **52** |
| `SetAttr` a file open for **Append** | **55** File already open |
| `SetAttr` a file open for **Input** | allowed |

### FileCopy

| Call | Result |
|---|---|
| `FileCopy a.txt, e.txt` | copied, length 3 |
| onto an existing file | overwritten |
| onto a read-only target | **75** |
| onto a **hidden** target | **75** |
| from a read-only source | the copy is **32**: the attributes are not copied, and the copy gets Archive |
| from a missing source | **53** |
| into a missing directory | **76** |
| onto a directory, or from a directory | **75** |
| onto itself | **70** Permission denied |
| with a wildcard in the source | **52** |
| from a file open for **Output** | **55** |
| onto a file open for Output | **55** |
| from a file open for **Input** | allowed |

### Name … As …

| Call | Result |
|---|---|
| `Name e.txt As f.txt` | renamed |
| onto an existing file | **58** File already exists |
| from a missing file | **53** |
| onto itself | no error |
| `f.txt As F.TXT` | renamed: `Dir` then lists `F.TXT` |
| a directory | renamed |
| into another directory | moved |
| into a **missing** directory | **53**, not 76 |
| with a wildcard | **52** |
| a file open for Input | **55** |
| a read-only file | renamed |

### Kill

| Call | Result |
|---|---|
| a file | deleted |
| a missing file, or `""` | **53** |
| `*.tmp`, matching 2 files | both deleted |
| `*.zzz`, matching nothing | **53** |
| `q?.dat` | both deleted |
| a **read-only** file | **75** |
| a **hidden** file, or a **system** file | **53**: `Kill` does not see them |
| `*.log` matching a hidden and a normal file | the normal one deleted, the hidden one kept, no error |
| a directory | **53** |
| a file open for Input | **55** |

### Dir

| Call | Result |
|---|---|
| `Dir()` before any `Dir(pattern)` | **5** Invalid procedure call or argument |
| `Dir()` after a listing has returned `""` | **5** |
| `Dir("*.txt")` | read-only files included, hidden and system left out. Order: `a,b,i,ko,n,n2,r,w,w2` |
| `Dir(p, 0)` | the same as `vbNormal` |
| `Dir(p, vbHidden)` | adds hidden files |
| `Dir(p, vbSystem)` | adds system files |
| `Dir(p, vbReadOnly)` | the same as `vbNormal` |
| `Dir(base & "\*", vbDirectory)` | `.`, `..`, then files and directories together, in name order |
| `Dir("*.htm")` | **`c.htm` and `d.html`**: the extension matches through the 8.3 short name |
| `Dir("?.txt")` | one-character names only |
| `Dir("A.TXT")` | `a.txt`: no case, and the name comes back as stored |
| `Dir` and `Dir$` | both String |
| `Dir(base, vbDirectory)` | `fx`, the directory's own name |
| `Dir(base)`, with no `vbDirectory` | `""` |
| `Dir(base & "\")` | the first file, `a.txt` |
| `Dir(base & "\", vbDirectory)` | `.` |
| no match, or a missing directory | `""`, not an error |
| `Dir("")` | the first file in `CurDir`. Here that is `err.log`, the `/make` log |
| `Dir("fx\a.txt")` | resolves against `CurDir` |
| `Dir("C:\", vbVolume)` | `""` here, but the guest's volume has no label, so this decides nothing |
| `Dir(base & "\*", vbVolume Or vbDirectory)` | `.`: with another bit, `vbVolume` acts as `vbDirectory` |
| attribute 1024, or -1 | **5** |
| `Dir(Null)` | **13** Type mismatch |
| `Dir("*.txt")`, then `Dir("*.htm")`, then `Dir()` | `d.html`: a new pattern restarts the listing |
| the listing's file `Kill`ed mid-listing, then `Dir()` | carries on to the next file |
